teaser.text: BT Group builds and runs communications networks, then sells connections and services over them. Its money comes from recurring payments by households, organisations and other communications providers, while much of its spending goes into networks that must be built before they can earn.

blocks.heading: Where could BT's shares be by October 2027?

paragraphs.text: The weighted forecast is 296.05 GBp in October 2027. That implies a +47% return. It reaches 352.57 GBp in October 2029. That implies a +82% return, including dividends. Bear has 32% probability. Base has 48%. Bull has 20%.

By October 2029, the bear case gives 189.99 GBp and the bull case gives 533.15 GBp. The probabilities are 32% for bear, 48% for base and 20% for bull. The base therefore offers the most likely route, but the valuation remains highly sensitive to cash delivery.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for BT, and what could go wrong?

paragraphs.text: The case improves when lower fibre construction spending lifts cash, fibre take-up holds up and customers stay. The CMA, the UK regulator that reviews whether mergers could harm competition, is due to report on TalkTalk on 19 October 2026. Conditions or a longer review could delay integration benefits. December 2026 tests the 25 million premises target. January 2027 tests the planned exit from the analogue telephone network. FY27 results must show whether EBITDA guidance and the £2,000 million cash target withstand TalkTalk’s costs and pension payments.

blocks.heading: How much cash does BT really make?

paragraphs.text: BT generates substantial operating cash, but investment, leases and interest absorb nearly all of it. Cash from operations was £7,030 million in FY2026. After cash capital spending of £5,169 million, lease payments of £731 million and interest of £1,028 million, only £102 million remained. Subtracting £49 million for stock pay gives £53 million of real free cash flow, an analytical measure that recognises the dilution cost of employee compensation.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for BT today?

paragraphs.text: BT trades on a forward P/E of 11.06x and a dividend yield of 4.0%. BT’s free cash flow yield is 0.5%, while its real free cash flow yield is 0.3%. Net debt rose from £12,729 million in FY22 to £16,695 million in FY26. Real free cash flow per share turned positive in FY26 but remained below dividends paid per share.

blocks.heading: How much does BT pay per share?

paragraphs.text: Base dividends rise from £0.0857 to £0.0910 per share. The bear holds at £0.0707, while the bull reaches £0.0964. The base applies 3% annual growth, consistent with BT's low-to-middle single-digit policy. The cut remains plausible because FY26 real free cash flow was only £53m and TalkTalk is expected to have a £400m FY27 cash impact.

blocks.heading: Does BT’s cash cover its dividend?

paragraphs.text: In March 2026, free cash flow was positive at £102m. Dividends were £807m and share purchases were £126m. The resulting shortfall was £831m. BT could meet it from cash reserves, investment sales or borrowing, but each choice reduced financial flexibility.

blocks.heading: What is BT’s dividend yield at its share price?

paragraphs.text: At 206.90p, shareholders value BT at £20,623.047m. Enterprise value estimates the cost of the operating business, including debt that a buyer would assume, and stands at £37,318.047m. The difference is £16,695m. BT’s net debt includes lease liabilities, which are future payments for leased assets, while net financial debt excludes them. The valuation therefore depends on using the correct debt measure.

Cash gives the harder test. BT reported £1,508m of normalised free cash flow and a 4.0% dividend yield. Its normalised measure deducts investment, interest and leases, but excludes pension deficit payments and specified costs. Those obligations still consume cash, so dividend safety depends on what remains after them.

blocks.heading: What has BT guided for the year?

paragraphs.text: Management guides to £2,000 million of normalised free cash flow in FY27 and roughly £3 billion by the end of the decade. Openreach targets 25 million FTTP premises by December 2026. FTTP means fibre-optic cables running all the way to a home or business. It also targets 800,000 broadband line losses in FY27. BT expects low-to-middle single-digit annual dividend growth; larger payments depend on stronger credit metrics and residual cash. TalkTalk is expected to have a £400 million FY27 cash impact, excluded from the existing free-cash-flow target.

EBITDA rises from £8,225m in October 2027 to £8,550m in October 2029. The bear path falls to £7,725m before a modest recovery, while the bull path reaches £8,950m. The base begins near FY27 guidance, which is £8,100m–£8,200m, and assumes fibre mix and savings gradually offset line losses and TalkTalk. Consumer EBITDA fell from £2,672m to £2,602m, but Openreach rose from £3,827m to £4,225m, supporting moderate improvement rather than a sharp decline. The 825,000 FY26 line losses and 800,000 FY27 guide explain the downside.

blocks.heading: Has BT kept its past promises?

paragraphs.text: In May 2025, Kirkby increased planned fibre construction and later reported that Openreach had delivered the accelerated programme. That shows execution, but building the network is not the same as earning a good return from it.

BT also reported £913 million of gross annualised savings during FY25 and £1.2 billion cumulatively after eighteen months. Annualised means the estimated yearly benefit once changes are fully in place, not necessarily the cash saved during that year. The savings support management’s execution record, but they matter to shareholders only if they endure without shifting costs into weaker service.

blocks.heading: What have BT’s revenue and profit done?

paragraphs.text: That explains the contrast between network progress and group revenue. Openreach full-fibre connections rose from 1.8 million in March 2022 to 8.8 million in March 2026, while group revenue fell from £20,850 million to £19,654 million over the same period. International revenue fell partly because BT sold businesses, while UK service revenue declined as traditional voice services shrank. Fewer handset sales also reduced turnover.
